The Slaty antwren (Myrmotherula schisticolor) is a small insectivorous passerine inhabiting the understory of humid montane forests from southern Mexico to western Ecuador. Neonates emerge from incubated eggs at a remarkably early developmental stage, with the time from fertilization to hatching lasting 15 days [ab = 15 days] when the egg is maintained at an ambient temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C]; this incubation period is relatively abbreviated compared to many other thamnophilids. Nestlings at the moment of hatching exhibit a minimal body mass of only 1.5 grams [Wwb = 1.5 grams], a value that places them among the lighter-bodied newborns within the Thamnophilidae and underscores the altricial nature of their development. The ultimate wet weight achieved by fully grown adults, in contrast, reaches approximately 9.6 grams [Wwi = approximately 9.6 grams], reflecting a roughly six-fold increase in mass from the neonatal stage. This pattern of modest birth weight followed by substantial somatic growth is characteristic of species that rely on intensive biparental provisioning during the nestling period.

Fledging, the critical transition from a brooded nestling dependent on parental feeding to an independent juvenile capable of flight, occurs quickly in this species. Under the stable thermal conditions typical of the antwren's active metabolic period, at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], young birds achieve their first flight and depart the nest at just 9 days [tx = 9 days] after hatching. This abbreviated nestling period is relatively short compared to many Neotropical passerines of similar adult body mass, a trait that may be linked to high nest predation pressure in the understory. Following fledging, the gonadal maturation process proceeds over a considerably longer timeline. Field observations and captive rearing studies indicate that puberty, defined by the onset of gametogenesis and reproductive activation, is attained at 69 days [tp = 69 days] after hatching when individuals are maintained at 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This interval represents a significant proportion of the juvenile phase and suggests a prolonged period of somatic development before reproductive competence is achieved.

Reproductive output in the Slaty antwren is characterized by a modest but consistent rate. Adult females typically produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], a clutch size that is small even by thamnophilid standards, and they complete two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year], restricting their breeding activity largely to the wet season when arthropod prey is most abundant. This yields a modest annual reproductive output, with most pairs successfully raising no more than two offspring annually. The age at first successful breeding event, representing the time since birth at which an individual produces its first brood, occurs relatively late given the species' body size. First reproduction is recorded at 365 days [tR = 365 days] after hatching under the typical thermal regime of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], a delay that likely reflects the need to acquire a territory and establish a pair bond in the dense, competitive understory environment.

Longevity records for the Slaty antwren indicate a maximum lifespan that is considerable for a bird of its diminutive size. The oldest documented individuals have been monitored for approximately 7.2 years, or roughly 2628 days [am = roughly 2628 days] from hatching, under conditions where ambient temperatures average around 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This extended lifespan is notable among small insectivores and suggests a life-history strategy oriented toward adult survival and repeated breeding attempts across multiple seasons, rather than maximizing single-season reproductive effort. Basal metabolic rate measurements, obtained from respirometry trials on wild-caught adults, provide a physiological correlate of this pace of life. At the standard thermoneutral temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the maximum resting oxygen consumption recorded was 45.45 milliliters per hour [JOi = 45.45 milliliters per hour], a value that is consistent with the allometric expectations for a 9.6 gram passerine and reflects the elevated energetic demands of maintaining a constant body temperature in the cool, humid montane environment.

The ecological and behavioral traits of the Slaty antwren are intimately linked to its life history schedule and the specific microclimatic conditions of its cloud forest habitat. The species is a typical understory gleaner, foraging in mixed-species flocks for spiders, beetles, and caterpillars among dead leaves and epiphytes, a foraging niche that necessitates strong parental care through both the nestling and early fledgling stages. The brief 9-day nestling period (9 days) [tx = 9 days] is a period of exceptionally rapid feather growth and mass gain, with altricial nestlings completely dependent on the parents for both thermoregulation and food delivery at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This rapid development is balanced by a notably extended post-fledging dependency period, during which juveniles continue to receive food from the parents while they hone their foraging skills.
